utterances.text: I didn't know that, Your Honours. I knew that they should not be humiliated and that they should not be put under any risk, and that was provided, but I didn't know of that particular element that you have just mentioned, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that you were authorised to release prisoners who had letter of guarantee from the third country and transit visa through Croatia, and to allow them to leave the prison and to be taken to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I raise the same objection as ten minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I guess the Prosecutor is at the last set of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour. You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have to repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that you were the only person authorised to decide the question on releasing prisoners from Dretelj and Gabela and to allow them to go through Croatia, via Croatia, to some third country, provided they had a guarantee letter from any third country and transit visa through Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely incorrect, Your Honours, but allow me to clarify. For a very short period of time, when I tried to assume responsibility and to regulate the situation in these camps, I asked for the investigative procedures to be accelerated and I asked for the people who had papers proving that they have somewhere to go and that they could be sent somewhere, I wanted to use my influence and help them leave the prison. And one of those groups was the group of those who wanted to go to a third country and already had a visa to go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do it on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would -- I was doing that for a very short period of time before the order arrived that I was not to be involved in the work of the military investigative organisations and that I was not involved in the work of Dretelj and Gabela. But I do believe that on several occasions, I tried to use my influence and help those for whom the investigative organs had established that they were not guilty of any crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 565.3, 566.11.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: The second document, 566.11.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first one?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: The first one, 565.3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you see these two documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I only have one document in front of me, so can you please give me some more time. Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you see that these documents were issued in August 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see your signature underneath of the documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the situation, when prisoners were released, with a guarantee letter and transit visa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seems so, Mr. Prosecutor. However, before that there should have been a security check to establish that they had not participated in combat, in the killings. And here you can see the signature of the chief of the security services, who issued this document, which I approved, using my influence to release these people. You remember that document, signed by the chief of police, in which it says that he maybe would accept my suggestion about the release of the prisoners. I was not the person in charge of the release of these detainees. I was the person who had some influence and used it with the security services when it was discussed whether some of these people would be released. Whether there was somebody else involved in that, from the ministry, from the Main Staff, from any of the other brigades, who could request that, I don't know. I believe that I did this, and I would do it again in order to protect these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, we also have Exhibits 571.1, 573.2, 583.2, 596.1, just identical content and with the same signatures, and in total, in total, 149 prisoners were released in this way.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can you repeat the numbers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor and Mr. Witness, with the consent of the President, I'd like to ask a question at this stage, before the point is lost, to ask a question of the witness. My understanding of what the witness has said in response to your numerous questions is that these were people who had been arrested and detained and who had been subject to investigation, and that the investigation had established that they were not guilty of any crimes. What I want you to answer, Witness, is if it had been established that these people were innocent of any crimes, why did they have to have documents to leave the country? Why were they not immediately released to their own homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I used my influence to get them released. That's what I know. These people, as far as I know - this is what I heard - obtained visas and documents. They wanted to leave the country. In other words, there was a group of people in the prison for whom I exerted my influence on their behalf so that they could be released as soon as possible if it had been established that they were not guilty of any crimes. That was my influence, the influence that I could exert. I didn't ask them to ask for any visas. I did not exert any pressure on them. They were released upon my intervention. I don't know whether they were all released even. This is just my opinion, my consent that these people should be released. Whether they were released, where they went from there, I don't know. I don't have any record on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You see, Witness, I want to know from you, if you can answer: Why, if it had been established that these people were guilty of no criminal offences, did they need consent to be released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honours. I think that we are talking at cross-purposes here. They did not need any consent. We have to start from the beginning. It should not have been proven first that they didn't do anything. But I asked my assistant for security -- when I heard that there was a large number of people there, that there was some crime going on there, I wanted to speed up some things. I wanted to alleviate the pain of some people. I asked for the procedure to be accelerated. And I was then approached by the chief of security services, with a list of people for whom they had established, allegedly, that they were not guilty. Then I would turn to the prison ward and ask them to speed up the release of these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you ever see any documents issued by the Croatian authorities just allowing for the prisoners to cross the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm doing this because of my conscience, because of my understanding of justice, my 25-year practice in being a lawyer, and because of my sense of justice. This cross-examination has been going on for four hours. Now, how are we going to finish eight witnesses in five days if we're going to tolerate this? But the truth is, Your Honours, that these questions are not at all relevant in relation to my client, at all. They have no relevance whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. At this moment, we don't see any relevance of this question to this very case, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have already advised you to cut short your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, this will be my final question now, final question, and my cross-examination will be accomplished. The last one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember any of the statements made by you when you claimed that: "We have no friends in the world except our fatherland Croatia, whose part we want to become"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, again we lost a link for a moment. Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember a statement made by you that: "The destiny of the Croatian people is in our hands. We have no friends in the world except our fatherland Croatia, whose part we want to become"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This, very simply, Mr. Prosecutor and Your Honours, is not correct. I have never stated anything like this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 611.12. This is information by information propaganda service of the 1st Knez Domagoj Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present at this meeting which was held on the 25th of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is clear, Your Honours, that I cannot remember such a meeting. I cannot remember this particular meeting which was supposedly held on the 25th of September. I can allow for the possibility that this meeting did take place, because sometimes, although rarely, such meetings did take place. Now, in order not to exaggerate, I believe that this meeting may have taken place once or twice a year. But to take this as some kind of evidence, I don't think that is correct. Nobody has signed this document, let alone myself, and not even from the information propaganda service. It is a question whether anyone had ever received this document. I believe that this is just an opinion of an individual from some kind of service, a propaganda service. He probably tried to do something like this and play with these kind of statements. And thirdly, if I had been doing this, would I then, Your Honours, already in 1994, and particularly in 1995, would I be in Sarajevo with these very same Muslims and Bosniaks trying to create one unified army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your patience. My cross-examination is over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any re-examination, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I don't have any additional questions. I have some objections regarding some documents but we can do that after they are being tendered. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions? Yes, Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I have one or two questions, sir, arising out of your evidence. In the early part of -- I think it was your direct examination with Mr. Krsnik, on a number of occasions, you have referred to documents or information which you received which proved to you that the -- either the Muslim faction of the HVO or the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was about to launch an attack against the HVO. Now, you referred to that on a number of occasions. Where did you actually get this information and when? It's obviously important, but it hasn't been elaborated on. Can you help us on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I agree that this is one of the most important matters. In my opinion, certainly it is. In my command, there was a person, a man who was responsible for gathering this kind of information, this man who attempted to try and build up some kind of intelligence service. He had his own network of people who were gathering pieces of information on all sides. And there was a department for electronic reconnaissance, and this department gathered, monitored the opponents' communications and messages, analysed them and drew conclusions from that. On the basis of their evaluations, their assessment, the information and announcements directly from Muslim soldiers, from Bosniaks and from their ranks, on the basis of the orders that came from their superior commands, of their analysis. And all of these documents should be in the Zagreb archive, that the press is going on about a great deal. Personally, when we captured half of the brigade, of the Bregava Brigade - and again, according to my judgement, I thought that they would attack us and that they were representing a threat - when we attacked them and captured them, we found the archive. We found all of their documents that they had written. We also found in their archive, not only -- not only through our service but we then managed to get hold of various kind of different interesting data. First of all, we found something, the order of Mr. Bajro Pizovic as -- attack, that there will be an order for the attack on us. We -- it will be easy to find such an order in the same archive in Zagreb. Second, there was the order of Mr. Arif Pasalic, and unless I'm very much mistaken, you have taken this with some reservations. This was the order for the attack of the operation Neretva in order to get -- to reach the sea. Further on, we found some lists of the Bregava Brigade members, and at the same time, checking those lists, we established that these people were members of my own brigade, which means that they were members of my brigade, and some other army also has them as members of their units. Now, is that strengthening any kind of confidence? That means, again, that these documents can be found in our intelligence services, in our departments, although these should be analysed carefully, and also from the Muslim Bosniak side, in their archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. As I understand what you've said, there are two sources for these documents: First of all, there would be electronic recordings of conversations that were overheard and then analysed; and secondly, there were seized documents. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think that we understood each other fully. What I meant was -- is that one command would make a decision on doing something, on launching an operation, for instance, on the basis of some arguments, some facts, certainly some assessments. Now, these assessments of the commander or to the commander is normally given by the military intelligence service, and his superiors can give this to the commander. Then the command has a meeting and, on the basis of all these arguments, makes an evaluation and decides upon an operation. This is exactly what we did. We then launched the operation, and when we captured part of this unit, we managed to find exactly this kind of evidence that we had discussed in this stage before the operation was launched. For instance, the order of Mr. Bajro Pizovic, the order to attack us. And this order was written before we launched our operation towards this brigade, which means, Your Honours, that this brigade was preparing to launch an operation, an attack on us. We knew about it and we therefore attacked them. In their archive we find the evidence that they were going to attack us. I propose that evidence should be looked for in the HVO archive and in the BH Army archive. And what the honourable judge mentioned is just one of the questions within this matter, how intelligence service gets hold of information, and intelligence service gets hold of information different ways. First of all, in the field, through people. A second one would be through electronic monitoring, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I just have to say, Witness, that I'm not cutting across you but it's coming up to 1.00 and the Court is obliged to take a break. Now, my questions won't take a great deal longer but they may elicit further questioning from your Defence counsel or from the Prosecution. So in deference to everybody, I think it would be appropriate if we were to take a break now. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will have the lunch break and we'll resume at 2.30 this afternoon. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to begin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I really didn't mean to ask you how intelligence was gathered, but really what I wanted to know was that, if I understand your evidence correctly, what you are saying is that there were two sources for your belief that an attack by the Muslim forces was imminent, and one was intelligence, and two was the subsequent retrieval of documents from captured soldiers. Am I correct about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and also the information from the superiors.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the entire answer given by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Did you hear that, sir, that the interpreters apparently didn't catch everything that you said? I think what has been typed out here is that you said that you received the information, you agreed with me, and also you received information from your superiors. Was there anything we missed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I take it, then, that on the basis of army intelligence and evidence and instructions from your superiors, you formed the decision to disarm the Muslim members of the HVO and to capture any ABiH soldiers in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I could agree with what you said. So we agreed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You see, the point I'm getting at is that when the decision was made to act as you did, you already, in your view, had sufficient information of the intent of the Muslim component of Bosnia and Herzegovina to justify your actions. You really didn't need any of the seized documents. Am I right about that? The subsequently seized documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely right, Your Honour. That means that these documents that we captured, they just supported the previous hypothesis that they were preparing to attack us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'm clear on what you're saying. Now, this may be more difficult. Could you give the Court a time frame for this activity? When did you first form the view that it was a military expedient to disarm the Muslim forces that you came in contact with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can try, Your Honour, to answer your question in trying to recollect, although I don't think that I will be able to remember all the elements. So that is that the tension between the HVO and the newly established army of BH grew on a daily basis. We witnessed also, and followed, what their political officials said, alongside everything I have already spoken about. The actual arming, in secret of the Muslim people - so that is very important - and this arming of the Muslim people you can now read about this in the books that are now being written by certain members of the then Muslim authorities. They also support the thesis that I've already mentioned. So they were arming only Muslims, and in this way they provoked tensions and lack of confidence. Furthermore, they infiltrated their people. The BH Army infiltrated people into my area. They communicated through radio link and they were given certain tasks. All of this we were able to decode. Moreover, Your Honour, I also had the opportunity to listen to the information and to get hold of minutes from meetings of civilian authorities subsequently. And these civilian authorities, what I mean is only Muslims, Bosniaks, who were members of the SDA party. And at those meetings, they tasked their operatives in the field to implement their decisions or to pass them on and to form their own army, independent, only army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and also to infiltrate HVO ranks, to equip themselves and to be ready to take us on, through force, and to enter into conflict with us. They also received instructions, Your Honour - and believe me, I do have evidence of that, and I can clarify this - they received instructions to take -- to loot ammunition from the HVO, to steal weapons and ammunition and to transfer these to the BH Army. Excuse me, this was just the beginning. And after that, what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for all the details that you're giving me of the intelligence which you gathered, but what I'm really trying to find out is the time frame at which you had enough information to make the decision to act as you did. When was the first -- the first direct act of disarming Muslim members of the HVO and arresting ABiH members? That's what I really want to know. I need a time frame for that because if I follow your evidence correctly - and I believe I do - at that stage, you had sufficient evidence to act as you -- as you did. You didn't rely on any documents which were subsequently obtained. So what I really want to know is what time are we talking about? Are we talking about late 1992, early 1993, or mid-1993? Can you recall? As best you can. If you can't, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really cannot tell you absolutely, with absolute precision, but I believe that this time was in the early -- early 1993, end of 1992, when we already had enough evidence in order to take the steps that we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is in relation to the documents. Did you actually see those documents or did you subsequently go to the Zagreb archive to retrieve them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never visited the Zagreb archive. I only know about the Zagreb archive from the press. And the documents that I'm talking about, some of them I saw them immediately after the archive of the Bregava Brigade was captured, was seized, and later on I saw some others subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, again, these are difficult questions for a military man. Can you put a time, approximate time, when you saw the documents which were seized from the Bregava Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the documents seized from the Bregava Brigade I saw on the following day, the day after some members of that brigade were captured. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And when was that? What month approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise if I'm mistaken, but I believe that it was in April, 1992. I apologise. It was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: April, 1993. Now, just to put things into context, I'm sure that you have heard a great deal about the events in Ahmici, which we know took place in the early part of April, 1993. If you can, could you say whether the seizure of the documents from the Bregava Brigade preceded or followed the tragic events in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really, really cannot remember that. I was never in that area. And all I can tell you is what I read or heard. I don't want to spread any rumours or speculations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Perhaps you misunderstand me. I don't want to you comment on Ahmici, but because it was an unusual event, shall we say that, that you might be able to place it in your calendar of events as being something that came after the capture of members of the Bregava Brigade or before it. But if you can't, you know, I can well understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can really not remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, you can't do any better than that. Can I ask a question in private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of the Judges' questions? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, Her Honour Diarra's question. You said, Mr. Witness, that you saw Mr. Naletilic in Medjugorje and then in Zagreb. What year was that when you first saw him in Medjugorje and then in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't say that for a fact. I think it was the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What year was that? 1994, 1995, 1996? What year was the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was the end of 1994, or maybe 1995 or 1996. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. And now I would ask you something that stems from Judge Clark's question, a very direct question. Do you maybe in your personal files have the order issued by Mr. Pizovic? I would be very grateful to you if you have it on you in Zagreb. If you have that order, maybe you could show it to us, or maybe you could give it to Madam Registrar in case you have it on you in Zagreb at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do have some documents on me. I don't know what documents I have, what documents are among my papers. I will check at the end of the day and see what I have, and I don't see a problem. If that order is indeed with me in Zagreb, I will leave it with your official, but I'm not sure that I have that order in Zagreb with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We have to follow a procedure. I don't know how much time it will take you to find it. Some documents have to be authenticated. I would be very grateful to you if this could be during this day, during your testimony, because if you leave it with Madam Registrar and if you do it tomorrow, then my learned friends from the Prosecution will object to that. So if you can do that now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the only thing left for me is if you could give me a break, during which I could check what documents I have on me, and then come back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, I would kindly ask you to check subsequently. We can't waste time on that. So if you do manage to find this order that was at length discussed today, please give it to our Madam Registrar, who will then bring it here to The Hague, and then we will see whether my learned colleagues will object to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And my final question. I'm sorry. This was not a question stemming from Judge Clark's questions, so this is not a question. I'm going to raise an objection when documents are tendered for admission. Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have only one question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, while preparing for your testimony, did you inform the counsel, counsel for the Defence, that you were in possession of some orders issued by ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this question stems from which question of one of the Honourable Judges?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Probably from your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: It's mine. That's mine. [Interpretation] Yes, from mine, certainly, because that is something I have raised. I know that Judge Clark asked questions about the archives, but this question certainly does not stem from any of the questions raised by any of the Honourable Judges. I'm sure I'm not mistaken in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I was going to ask you that question, but I've been pre-empted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you may answer that question, since this document, or this order, might be submitted to this courtroom at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't recall ever having discussed that issue with the counsel, and I don't remember ever telling him what documents I had. I am now prepared to deliver some of the documents that I find interesting, only their copies, because their originals have been officially archived. I have what I have, and I will leave it with you for your disposal and perusal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, thank you very much for your coming to help us. We all wish you good luck in your future. The usher will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, are there any documents to tender through this witness? Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, since I've got a number of documents that I intend to tender, I would like your -- to ask to give me permission just to file a submission with all the documents that I will tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that through this witness you used about 30 documents, so you're entitled to have some time to reorganise these documents and submit to this Trial Chamber whatever documents you are intending to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So this is the last witness through the videolink. And are there any other matters that both parties would like to address to this Trial Chamber? Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Just two brief matters to raise, the first of which is a follow-up to an issue that was raised in the proceedings that occurred on Monday. The Trial Chamber may recall that at the conclusion of the testimony of Witness NU, Mr. Bos, on behalf of the Prosecution, tendered a number of documents into evidence. The Defence raised questions as to four of the documents, particularly the source of the documents, whether they were Croatian government, the archive, or what have you, and I attempted at the time to supply some clarification. But we followed up on this. I'm talking about Exhibits 698.1, 699.1, 700.2, and 702.2. I can confirm for the Trial Chamber, and also for our learned friends on the Defence bench, that these four exhibits are documents that were provided to the ICTY field office in Zagreb in November of 2001, directly from the Croatian government's office for cooperation with the Tribunal. Particularly, a gentleman named Orsat Miljenic, who was in charge of that office, provided those documents to our field office in Zagreb. This would have been in response to a request for assistance issued by this office to the Croatian government. And the only other matter, Mr. President, was to inquire for a little clarification about the -- how the Trial Chamber intends to proceed during the first two days of next week. We have a videolink witness scheduled for Monday morning. The Trial Chamber's existing scheduling order allots two hours of time for that. And then we have a witness for Mr. Naletilic who is scheduled to appear before the Trial Chamber on Tuesday. And our question was whether the Trial Chamber then intends to move directly into hearing witnesses who are -- have come to testify as part of the case in chief for Mr. Martinovic, whether the Trial Chamber envisions proceeding with those witnesses on Tuesday or whether there will be a suspension of the hearing both on Monday and Tuesday afternoon and then starting with Mr. Martinovic's witnesses on Wednesday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as you all understand, that on Monday and Tuesday, this Trial Chamber only has half days, which means we could only sit until 1.45 in the afternoon. So we will do our best to finish that videolink conference witness on Monday. After that, on Tuesday, we will hear the remaining witness for Mr. Naletilic, live. And right after hearing of this witness, we will hear other witnesses in Mr. Martinovic's case. I hope we could finish that witness on Tuesday. Let's keep our hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to take a few minutes to inform the Honourable Judges about some concerns that the Defence has at the moment. Firstly, let me respond to honourable Judge Clark. Honourable Judge Clark, if I had this document that is so important for the Defence, don't you think I would tender it through this witness? But Judge Clark, these documents are held by the Prosecution. They are exculpatory for my client. I claim before you that they have those documents, not only those but the complete documentation by the BH Army. The Muslim component has refused to give them to me. The Deputy Minister of Defence has forbidden the minister to give me the BH Army documentation. I'm still preparing a large, huge file on the Bosnian and Herzegovinian government. I am preparing a huge submission for the honourable Trial Chamber and I will include this matter into that file that I'm preparing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Krsnik. That's a different issue. You see, your witness said that these documents are very readily available and that anybody could get them. And that's why I wondered why, when -- I don't know if you've been in Zagreb, but why you didn't ask somebody to get them if they are so readily available. We'd like to see them. We are not talking about documents that are held in Bosnia. I'm talking about documents which this witness gave sworn evidence on, their easy availability in Zagreb. They are the documents I'm asking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm very glad that you have raised this issue. I hope you will not hold it against me when I say that you may not be well-informed. The Zagreb archive holds thousands upon thousands of documents. I've been here in this courtroom for 14 months. I don't have so many people available to me as the Prosecution has. They have 20 people who can go there and look for a document. If you want to find a document, you have to go there and find it yourself, if such a document indeed exists in the Zagreb archive. I'm sure that that document does exist in Sarajevo but I don't have access to it, but I would not trouble you with that. I'm just talking about the equality of treatment that has been extended to both sides. I can't go to Zagreb archive and tell them, "Give me that document," because I don't know whether it exists. The documentation hasn't been properly classified. So it is very difficult for me to do that. But what I wanted to say is I have sent a submission to the honourable Court. I don't know whether you have received it. This submission concerns the request that we have for the Prosecution to deliver to us the BH Army documentation. We know that they have them. They have given them to other Defence counsel in other cases. And I believe that we also have the right to have an insight into that documentation. And thirdly, to my greatest concern, we've received documents that are part of the disclosure, and there are also some documents there of exculpatory nature. If I had had them during my cross-examination, then my cross-examination would have looked completely different. The documents that I received two days ago are very interesting and talk about the 9th of May and about the Muslim attack. I received those from the Prosecution. This has been to the huge detriment of the Defence. It is their duty to provide them to me at the beginning of this trial. The same goes to Sovici file which I got only upon your order. If I had had it earlier, my cross-examination would have looked differently. The Defence has been damaged by that, and some witnesses, I announce it now, some witnesses will be recalled for cross-examination for -- because we did not have all the documents available to us in time. That is all I wanted to say. And I wouldn't trouble you with that any longer. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, we -- it seems to me that we know next to nothing about that further disclosure of the documents. Would you please shed some light on this very issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Consistent with the Prosecution's continuing obligation to disclose documents and evidence to the Defence under the rules, a disclosure was made, I believe, last week or two weeks ago, and beyond that, I can't really add anything. We don't characterise them one way or another, whether they fall under Rule 68 or not. They are simply documents that were potentially falling within that category and they were disclosed. I think it is something that is a continuing obligation that we always have and will always observe. I think -- not having the documents in front of me, I've reviewed them, but I think it's really pointless at this point to go into any further discussion about the -- where to go from here or whether in fact it goes nowhere. On the Sovici file, this is a reference to the Mostar High Court file which was disclosed several months ago. The Trial Chamber will recall the pleadings in respect of that disclosure. We've never heard any response from the Defence whatsoever. Certainly, there has never been any suggestion on the part of the Defence of any prejudice that was suffered in respect of the Sovici or the Mostar High Court file. So we are really not in a position to respond to counsel's assertions about that. Just to briefly respond to some of the other points made, at the beginning of his remarks, counsel asserted that the Prosecution has these documents seized from the Bregava Brigade. Counsel has no basis for making such an assertion. He doesn't know. He's making an assertion that's based completely on speculation. The archive in Zagreb is open to everyone. Mr. Krsnik can have his investigators go there. And the one thing we agree on is the fact that at the Zagreb archive, they don't go fetch your documents for you. They treat the Prosecution people the same way that they treat the Defence people. Everyone has to go do it the hard way, which is to look through binders and to request copies of documents of relevance. We are treated the same way in Zagreb that the Defence are. There is complete equality in that respect. Moreover, there is equality in respect of the resources available to both parties to send people, to dispatch people, to Zagreb to review those archives. The number that has continually been asserted, 20 people in the archive, is simply wrong. We don't have 20 people in the archive. We don't have anyone in the archive these days. We simply don't have the means to do it. Third, the assertion that the documents are somehow in the custody of the archive of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it's not clear to me how documents of the ABiH that were seized by a unit of the HVO could have landed now in Sarajevo in the archive of the Armija. So it's not clear to me what point there is in even raising the issue of counsel's alleged difficulties with the Armija's archive in Sarajevo. Those are my comments, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we are not debating here. I give you one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't take any longer. Of course it is in the Armija's archive because every order is issued in several copies and sent to various addresses. So I'm sure that all the orders are in the Armija's archives because no single order is issued in one copy. The Sovici file, as you know, we don't have investigators in the pre-trial stage, and our investigators are paid by us, by the Defence, and we do not have a team of investigators available to us. In my efforts travelling to Mostar to do my own investigations -- can we please move to private session? Because everything we say here in the courtroom is immediately conveyed. As soon as the Muslim side learns what we are up to, they try to hide things. I've come across such things on the ground so many times before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise. May I just say for the record that the Prosecution submits that's not a sufficient ground for moving out of public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Anyway, we will go to private session so Mr. Krsnik can explain to us the very reason for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, although the Rules of Procedure and Evidence upholds the principle of equality of arms, I'm quite sympathetic with the position of the Defence counsel, because in practice, the Defence counsel will meet more difficulties in obtaining the evidence and documents. Since you have already submitted some motions on filings to this Trial Chamber, we'll act after we read your filings and to see whether there's any material damage to the interests of the Defence counsel. Are there anything else? Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, just on that last point, Mr. President, it's my recollection, at least, that the initial filings of the Defence in respect of the Mostar High Court file were filed on an ex parte basis and were then subsequently disclosed to the Prosecution, and we were then in a position to respond. Because, as I understand it, the assertion is going to be that there has been some prejudice to the Defence in their ability to cross-examine Prosecution witnesses, for example, I would request the Trial Chamber to order that any submissions along these lines be provided to the Prosecution as well as to the Trial Chamber, and not be filed on an ex parte basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll take note of your request. Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will be very brief. What is not clear, the question that has remained unclear, in relation to the documentation that has recently been handed over by the Croatian government - that is what Mr. Stringer said - the office for cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. So I think this is slightly unclear in relation to the request that we have asked, to have all the documentation. Did the Prosecutor's office receive a large number of documents, or did they select it, or did they already receive selected documents from the office for cooperation? The reason why I'm asking this is because the Defence for Vinko Martinovic asked precisely the documentation from the office for cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, and we haven't received anything. So now perhaps we could hear from our learned colleagues from the Prosecution about our request, whether did they receive a large file of documents and they selected, or was this already selected when they received it, so that we know where we stand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we were informed that only four or five documents were the requested documents among the documents used by the Witness NU. Is there any more information?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I frankly don't know whether these documents, these four documents, came across with additional documents. I don't know. I wasn't involved in that particular request for assistance. I don't know if I misunderstood counsel. He indicated that they've requested documents, and I just think it's -- to be clear, there's never been a request to the Prosecution for disclosure of anything in this case from the Defence. This goes back to the very beginning. The strategic decision was made years ago not to request disclosure from the Prosecution of documents material to the preparation of the case. The only disclosure obligations on the Prosecution in this case are those that arise under Rule 68. Now, if the Defence has made a request of these documents from the Croatian government - maybe that's what he's saying - I certainly wouldn't have any involvement or knowledge of that, and I'm not in a position to speak on behalf of the Croatian government in respect of any Defence requests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So that's all for today. We'll resume next Monday, 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 2nd day of September, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
